# Unit 2: Web technologies and databases Most drug information today is looked up on web pages and stored in databases. This unit explains how the web works (HTML, XML, CSS, programming languages, web servers and server products) and then how databases store and find data (database concepts, MySQL, MS Access and pharmacy drug databases). ## 2.1 The Internet and the World Wide Web - **Internet** — a worldwide network of computer networks that exchange data using the TCP/IP set of rules (protocols). - **World Wide Web (WWW)** — a service on the Internet made of linked documents (web pages) viewed in a **web browser** (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari). It was proposed by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989. - **Web page** — one document written in HTML; a **website** is a group of related pages under one domain. - **URL** (uniform resource locator) — the address of a resource, e.g. `https://www.example.org/drugs/index.html` = protocol + domain name + path. - **HTTP** (hypertext transfer protocol) — the rule for requesting and sending web pages. **HTTPS** is the secure, encrypted version, needed wherever patient data or passwords are sent. - **Client–server model** — the browser (client) sends a request; the web server returns the page. ```text BROWSER (client) WEB SERVER user types URL ── HTTP request ──► finds the file or runs a program (may query a database server) shows the page ◄── HTTP response ── sends HTML, CSS, images, scripts ``` ## 2.2 HTML (HyperText Markup Language) **HTML** is the language used to create the structure and content of web pages. It is a **markup language**, not a programming language: it uses **tags** to mark parts of a document (heading, paragraph, list, table, link, image). The browser reads the tags and displays the page. **Features** - Tags are written in angle brackets: `

` opens and `

` closes. A tag plus its content is an **element**. - Some tags are empty (no closing tag): `
`, ``, `
`. - Tags can have **attributes** that give extra information: ``, ``. - HTML tags are predefined (fixed) and not case-sensitive. The current version is **HTML5**. - Files are saved with the extension `.html` or `.htm` and opened in a browser. **Basic structure of an HTML document** ```text Drug Information

Paracetamol

Class: Analgesic and antipyretic

  • Dosage form: tablet
  • Store below 25 °C
More information ``` **Common tags** | Tag | Use | | --- | --- | | ``, ``, ``, `<body>` | Document structure; title appears on the browser tab | | `<h1>` to `<h6>` | Headings, largest to smallest | | `<p>`, `<br>`, `<hr>` | Paragraph, line break, horizontal line | | `<b>`, `<i>`, `<u>` | Bold, italic, underline | | `<ul>`, `<ol>`, `<li>` | Unordered (bullet) list, ordered (numbered) list, list item | | `<table>`, `<tr>`, `<th>`, `<td>` | Table, row, header cell, data cell | | `<a href="">` | Hyperlink | | `<img src="" alt="">` | Image | | `<form>`, `<input>`, `<select>`, `<button>` | Forms for entering data | | `<div>`, `<span>` | Containers used for layout and styling | ## 2.3 XML (eXtensible Markup Language) **XML** is a markup language designed to **store and carry data** in a form that both people and computers can read. In XML the writer **makes up the tags** to describe the data, so it is "extensible". ```text <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <drugs> <drug id="D001"> <name>Amoxicillin</name> <class>Penicillin antibiotic</class> <form>Capsule</form> <strength unit="mg">500</strength> </drug> </drugs> ``` **Rules of XML (a "well-formed" document)** 1. There must be exactly one **root element** that contains all others (`<drugs>` above). 2. Every opening tag must have a closing tag. 3. Tags are **case-sensitive** (`<Name>` and `<name>` differ). 4. Elements must be properly nested (close the inner element first). 5. Attribute values must be in quotes. The structure of an XML document can be fixed with a **DTD** or an **XML Schema (XSD)**; a document that follows it is called **valid**. **Uses:** exchanging data between different software (for example sending drug data from a database to a website), configuration files, the structured product information files used in regulatory submissions, and exporting Access tables (practical 12). **HTML vs XML** | HTML | XML | | --- | --- | | Displays data (how it looks) | Stores and carries data (what it is) | | Tags are predefined | Tags are defined by the user | | Not case-sensitive | Case-sensitive | | Browsers tolerate some missing closing tags | Every tag must be closed; strict rules | | Used for web pages | Used for data exchange and storage | ## 2.4 CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) **CSS** controls the **presentation** of HTML pages: colours, fonts, sizes, spacing, borders and layout. HTML gives structure; CSS gives style. Keeping style separate means one style sheet can format a whole website, and changing one file changes every page. **Syntax:** `selector { property: value; }` ```text h1 { color: navy; font-size: 24px; } p { font-family: Arial; line-height: 1.5; } .warning { color: red; font-weight: bold; } (a class, used as class="warning") #header { background-color: #e0f0ff; } (an id, used as id="header") ``` **Three ways to add CSS** | Type | Where | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Inline | In the tag's `style` attribute | `<p style="color:red">` | | Internal (embedded) | In a `<style>` block inside `<head>` | `<style> p {color:red;} </style>` | | External | In a separate `.css` file linked to every page | `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` | "Cascading" means that when several rules apply to one element, a fixed order of priority decides which one wins (inline beats internal, which beats external, and more specific selectors beat general ones). ## 2.5 Programming languages A **program** is a set of instructions for a computer; a **programming language** is the set of words and rules used to write it. | Generation | Type | Features | Examples | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1st | Machine language | Binary code; runs directly; machine-dependent; hard to write | 10110000 01100001 | | 2nd | Assembly language | Short codes (mnemonics) like ADD, MOV; needs an **assembler** | Assembly for a given processor | | 3rd | High-level languages | English-like, machine-independent; need a compiler or interpreter | C, C++, Java, Python, FORTRAN, COBOL | | 4th | Very high-level / query languages | Say *what* is wanted, not how | SQL, report generators | | 5th | Logic / constraint languages | Used in expert systems | Prolog | **Language translators** - **Assembler** — assembly language to machine code. - **Compiler** — translates the whole high-level program at once into machine code, then it runs (C, C++). - **Interpreter** — translates and runs one line at a time (Python, JavaScript); easier to test, usually slower. **Languages of the web** - **Client-side** (run in the browser): HTML, CSS, **JavaScript** (makes pages interactive — checking a form before it is sent, showing a drop-down). - **Server-side** (run on the web server): PHP, Python, Java, C# (ASP.NET), Node.js (JavaScript on the server). They read databases and build pages on request. - **SQL** talks to the database. ## 2.6 Web servers and server products A **web server** is a computer, and the software on it, that stores websites and sends pages to browsers in reply to HTTP requests. It runs all the time, has a fixed address and is connected to the Internet (or to a hospital's internal network, an **intranet**). **Common web server software** | Product | Notes | | --- | --- | | Apache HTTP Server | Free, open-source; long one of the most used servers; often run with Linux, MySQL and PHP (the "LAMP" stack) | | Nginx | Free, open-source; fast; often used in front of other servers | | Microsoft IIS (Internet Information Services) | Comes with Windows Server; runs ASP.NET sites | | Apache Tomcat | Runs Java web applications | **Server products** are server programs that provide other services on a network: - **Database servers** — MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle Database, PostgreSQL. - **Application servers** — run the business logic of large programs (hospital information system, ERP). - **Mail servers** — send and store e-mail (Microsoft Exchange). - **File and print servers**, **proxy servers** (filter and speed up web access), **DNS servers** (turn domain names into IP addresses). - **Cloud services** — servers rented over the Internet instead of bought (hosting, storage, databases). ## 2.7 Introduction to databases - **Database** — an organised collection of related data stored so it can be easily found, added to and changed. Example: a pharmacy's records of drugs, suppliers, patients and sales. - **DBMS (database management system)** — software that creates and manages databases and controls who can use them. Examples: MySQL, Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server, MS Access. **Why a database is better than separate files (advantages of a DBMS)** 1. Less **redundancy** (data stored once, not in many registers). 2. **Consistency** — one change updates everywhere. 3. **Data sharing** among many users at once. 4. **Security** — passwords and user rights. 5. **Integrity** — rules stop wrong entries (quantity cannot be negative). 6. Fast **searching and reports** through queries. 7. **Backup and recovery**. **Database models** | Model | Structure | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Hierarchical | Tree (one parent, many children) | Early IBM IMS | | Network | Records linked many-to-many | Older mainframe systems | | Relational (RDBMS) | Tables with rows and columns, linked by keys | MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, Access | | Object-oriented | Data stored as objects | Used for complex data such as images | **Relational database terms** | Term | Meaning | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Table (relation) | Data about one subject in rows and columns | `Drug` table | | Record (row, tuple) | All data about one item | One drug | | Field (column, attribute) | One kind of data | `DrugName`, `Strength` | | Data type | Kind of value in a field | Text, number, date, yes/no | | Primary key | Field that uniquely identifies each record; cannot be blank or repeated | `DrugID` | | Foreign key | Field in one table that refers to the primary key of another | `SupplierID` in the `Drug` table | | Relationship | Link between tables | One supplier → many drugs (one-to-many) | Relationships may be **one-to-one** (patient ↔ medical record number), **one-to-many** (one doctor writes many prescriptions) or **many-to-many** (many patients take many drugs, handled through a linking table such as `Prescription`). **Normalisation** is splitting data into well-designed tables so each fact is stored once, avoiding repetition and update errors. ```text SUPPLIER table DRUG table +-------------+-----------+ +--------+------------+----------+-------------+ | SupplierID | Name | | DrugID | DrugName | Strength | SupplierID | | (PK) | | | (PK) | | | (FK) | +-------------+-----------+ +--------+------------+----------+-------------+ | S1 | ABC Pharma| 1 ──► M | D1 | Metformin | 500 mg | S1 | | | | | D2 | Amlodipine | 5 mg | S1 | +-------------+-----------+ +--------+------------+----------+-------------+ One supplier (S1) supplies many drugs: a one-to-many relationship through SupplierID. ``` ## 2.8 SQL (Structured Query Language) **SQL** is the standard language for working with relational databases. | Group | Commands | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | DDL (data definition) | CREATE, ALTER, DROP | Make or change the structure of tables | | DML (data manipulation) | INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT | Add, change, remove and read data | | DCL (data control) | GRANT, REVOKE | Give or take away permissions | ```text CREATE TABLE Drug ( DrugID INT PRIMARY KEY, DrugName VARCHAR(50), Category VARCHAR(30), Stock INT ); INSERT INTO Drug VALUES (1, 'Metformin', 'Antidiabetic', 200); SELECT DrugName, Stock FROM Drug WHERE Stock < 50 ORDER BY DrugName; UPDATE Drug SET Stock = 180 WHERE DrugID = 1; DELETE FROM Drug WHERE DrugID = 1; ``` ## 2.9 MySQL **MySQL** is an open-source relational database management system that uses SQL. It is now owned by Oracle Corporation and is free under its community licence. - Works on the **client–server** model: the MySQL server holds the data; many clients connect at once. - Runs on Windows, Linux and macOS; fast and reliable for large numbers of records. - Supports user accounts and permissions, indexes, transactions and backups. - Widely used behind websites, often with PHP and Apache (LAMP), and through tools such as MySQL Workbench or phpMyAdmin. - **Pharmacy uses:** online pharmacy websites, hospital and pharmacy management software, drug information portals, storing clinical or laboratory data for many users. ## 2.10 MS Access **Microsoft Access** is a desktop relational DBMS that is part of Microsoft Office. It suits small offices, pharmacies and student projects. Databases are saved as one file (`.accdb`; older versions `.mdb`). **Objects of an Access database** | Object | Use | | --- | --- | | Table | Stores the data in rows and columns | | Query | Asks a question of the data: select, sort, filter, calculate, update or delete records | | Form | A screen for entering, viewing and editing records one at a time | | Report | Formatted output for printing (with groups, totals, headings) | | Macro | A saved series of actions to automate a task | | Module | Program code written in VBA (Visual Basic for Applications) | **Common data types in Access:** Short Text, Long Text, Number, Date/Time, Currency, AutoNumber, Yes/No, Attachment, Hyperlink, Lookup. **Views:** Datasheet view (enter data like a spreadsheet) and Design view (set fields, data types and the primary key). Tools such as the **Table, Form, Report and Label wizards** make objects step by step. **MySQL vs MS Access** | MS Access | MySQL | | --- | --- | | Desktop database in one file | Client–server database | | Few users at once; small data | Many users; large data | | Built-in forms and reports with a graphical interface | Needs other tools or programs for forms and reports | | Part of Microsoft Office (paid) | Free community edition, open-source | ## 2.11 Pharmacy drug databases A **drug database** is an organised, searchable collection of information on medicines: names (generic and brand), composition, dosage forms and strengths, indications, dose, contraindications, side effects, interactions, use in pregnancy and lactation, storage, price and manufacturer. **Uses in pharmacy** - Answering drug information queries from doctors, nurses and patients. - Checking prescriptions for drug interactions, duplications and wrong doses. - Finding substitutes and brands; stock and price lookup at the counter. - Patient counselling leaflets and labels. - Research, teaching and pharmacovigilance. **Examples** | Database | Type of information | | --- | --- | | National Formulary of India (NFI) | Government reference on drugs used in India | | CIMS and similar Indian drug indexes | Brands, composition, prices and prescribing data for Indian products | | DrugBank | Drug and drug-target data, chemistry and pharmacology (free for non-commercial use) | | PubChem (NCBI) | Chemical structures and properties of compounds | | Micromedex, Lexicomp | Clinical drug references used in hospitals (subscription) | | MEDLINE / PubMed | Published medical and pharmacy literature | **Hospital and pharmacy software** keeps its own drug master database, linked to stock, billing and patient records, so that the same drug data are used for dispensing, labelling and reports. ## Remember - Internet = network of networks; WWW = linked pages on it; URL = address; HTTP/HTTPS = rules for sending pages. - HTML = structure with predefined tags; XML = data with user-defined, case-sensitive tags and one root element; CSS = style (inline, internal, external). - Generations of languages: machine → assembly → high-level → 4GL (SQL) → 5GL; compiler translates all at once, interpreter line by line. - Web servers: Apache, Nginx, IIS, Tomcat; server products include database, application, mail, proxy and DNS servers. - Database = organised data; DBMS manages it; relational model uses tables, primary keys and foreign keys. - SQL: DDL (CREATE), DML (INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE), DCL (GRANT). - MS Access objects: tables, queries, forms, reports, macros, modules. - Drug databases support drug information, prescription checking, counselling and research.

# Unit 3: Applications of computers in pharmacy

Computers are now part of almost every pharmacy task: storing and finding drug information, calculating pharmacokinetic values, designing new molecules, running hospital and clinical pharmacy services, prescribing electronically, identifying medicines by barcode, dispensing automatically and helping patients take their medicines. This unit covers each application named in the syllabus, together with diagnostic, laboratory, patient-monitoring and pharma information systems.

## 3.1 Overview: where computers are used

| Area | Examples of use |
| --- | --- |
| Community pharmacy | Billing, stock control, expiry tracking, patient records, drug interaction alerts |
| Hospital and clinical pharmacy | Hospital information system, e-prescribing, unit-dose dispensing, therapeutic drug monitoring, adverse drug reaction reporting |
| Industry | Drug design, formulation development, production control, quality control data, documentation |
| Research | Pharmacokinetic modelling, statistics, bioinformatics, literature search |
| Regulation and education | Online submissions, drug databases, e-learning |

## 3.2 Drug information storage and retrieval

**Drug information** means accurate, up-to-date facts about medicines given to health professionals and patients. A **drug information centre** answers queries about doses, interactions, side effects, use in pregnancy, compatibility and identification of tablets.

**Storage** — information is kept in electronic databases instead of books and files:

- Tertiary sources: drug compendia, formularies and drug databases (National Formulary of India, Indian drug indexes, Micromedex, Lexicomp).
- Secondary sources: indexing and abstracting services (MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase) that point to articles.
- Primary sources: original research articles in online journals.
- The centre's own records of queries and answers, stored for reuse.

**Retrieval** — finding the needed information quickly by searching:

- Search by generic name, brand, class, indication or keyword.
- Use **Boolean operators**: AND (narrows: *metformin AND pregnancy*), OR (widens: *paracetamol OR acetaminophen*), NOT (excludes).
- Use filters (year, language, study type) and controlled vocabulary such as MeSH terms in PubMed.

**Steps in answering a query with a computer**

```text
Receive query → classify it and collect patient details → search tertiary source
     → if needed, secondary and primary sources → evaluate the evidence
     → give the answer (oral/written) → document the query and answer in the database
```

**Advantages:** speed, large storage in little space, easy updating, many users at once, search by many fields, records available for audit and teaching. **Limitations:** cost of subscriptions and hardware, need for training, dependence on power and Internet, risk of outdated or unreliable online information.

## 3.3 Computers in pharmacokinetics

**Pharmacokinetics** studies what the body does to a drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME). It needs many calculations on plasma concentration–time data, which computers do quickly and accurately.

**Uses**

1. **Calculating parameters** from concentration–time data: Cmax, tmax, area under the curve (AUC, by the trapezoidal rule), elimination rate constant (k), half-life (t½ = 0.693/k), clearance, volume of distribution and bioavailability.
2. **Fitting models** — choosing a one- or two-compartment model, or a non-compartmental analysis, and fitting the data by non-linear regression.
3. **Simulation** — predicting plasma levels for a new dose, dosing interval or route before giving it.
4. **Dosage regimen design and individualisation** — adjusting doses for kidney or liver disease, age and weight; used in **therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)** of narrow therapeutic index drugs such as digoxin, aminoglycosides, phenytoin, lithium and vancomycin.
5. **Population pharmacokinetics** — studying how parameters vary between patients using data from many people.
6. **Bioavailability and bioequivalence studies** — calculating and statistically comparing AUC and Cmax of test and reference products.
7. **Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models** — models built from organ blood flows and volumes to predict drug levels in organs.

**Software examples:** spreadsheets (MS Excel) for simple calculations, and specialised programs such as Phoenix WinNonlin and NONMEM used in industry and research.

```text
Plasma concentration
   |        * Cmax
   |      *    *
   |    *         *          AUC = area under this curve
   |  *              *  *
   |*                      *  *
   +----------------------------------- time
        tmax
```

## 3.4 Mathematical models in drug design

Discovering a drug by making and testing thousands of compounds is slow and costly. **Computer-aided drug design (CADD)** uses mathematical and computer models to predict which molecules are likely to work before they are made.

**1. Quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR)**

QSAR relates biological activity to measurable properties of molecules through an equation. The best known is the **Hansch approach**, which links activity (often written as log 1/C, where C is the concentration giving a fixed effect) to:

- **Lipophilicity** — partition coefficient (log P) or the substituent constant π;
- **Electronic effects** — the Hammett constant σ;
- **Steric (size) effects** — Taft's constant Es or molar refractivity.

A typical form is: log 1/C = a·π + b·σ + c·Es + d (a, b, c and d are found by regression; a squared π term is added when activity rises and then falls with lipophilicity). Once the equation is known, activity of new molecules can be predicted. **3D-QSAR** methods (such as CoMFA) use the three-dimensional fields around the molecules.

**2. Molecular modelling**

- **Molecular mechanics** — treats atoms as balls and bonds as springs to find the lowest-energy shape (conformation).
- **Quantum mechanics** — calculates electron distribution and reactivity for more accurate, slower results.
- **Molecular dynamics** — simulates how molecules move over time.

**3. Structure-based design** (when the 3D structure of the target protein is known, e.g. from X-ray crystallography in the Protein Data Bank):

- **Docking** — fits candidate molecules into the binding site and scores how well they bind.
- **Virtual screening** — docks large libraries of compounds by computer to pick a few for testing.

**4. Ligand-based design** (when the target structure is unknown): **pharmacophore** models (the 3D arrangement of features needed for activity, such as a hydrogen-bond donor, an aromatic ring and a positive charge) and similarity searching.

**5. ADMET prediction** — estimating absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity from structure, e.g. checking Lipinski's rule of five for oral drugs (molecular weight not more than 500, log P not more than 5, not more than 5 hydrogen-bond donors and not more than 10 acceptors).

**Advantages:** fewer compounds to synthesise, lower cost, shorter discovery time, better understanding of how drugs bind. Computer predictions must still be confirmed by laboratory and clinical tests.

## 3.5 Computers in hospital and clinical pharmacy

A **hospital information system (HIS)** links all departments (registration, wards, laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, billing). The **pharmacy module** handles:

- **Inventory control** — purchase orders, receipt, stock levels, reorder alerts, batch and expiry tracking, ABC/VED analysis.
- **Dispensing** — to outpatients and to wards (floor stock, individual prescription and **unit-dose** systems); labels and records.
- **Patient medication profiles** — all current and past drugs, allergies, weight, laboratory results.
- **Clinical decision support** — alerts for drug–drug interactions, drug–allergy problems, duplicate therapy, dose limits and renal dose adjustment.
- **Clinical pharmacy services** — medication review, TDM calculations, total parenteral nutrition calculations, intravenous admixture records.
- **Pharmacovigilance** — recording and reporting adverse drug reactions (in India to the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India).
- **Formulary management**, drug use evaluation, billing and statistical reports for the pharmacy and therapeutics committee.
- **Narcotic and psychotropic registers** kept electronically with audit trails.

## 3.6 Electronic prescribing and discharge (EP) systems

**Electronic prescribing (e-prescribing)** means the prescriber enters the prescription into a computer instead of writing it, and it is sent electronically to the pharmacy. In hospitals it is often part of **computerised physician (provider) order entry (CPOE)**. An **electronic discharge** system produces the discharge prescription and summary for the patient and the next care provider.

**How it works**

```text
Doctor selects drug, dose, route, frequency on screen
      → system checks allergies, interactions, dose range (decision support)
      → order sent to pharmacy electronically
      → pharmacist verifies and dispenses
      → nurse records administration on the electronic chart
      → at discharge: discharge prescription + summary printed/sent to patient and family doctor
```

**Benefits**

- No problems from illegible handwriting; complete orders (no missing dose or route).
- Fewer medication errors through automatic checks.
- Faster communication between doctor, pharmacy and nurse.
- Complete medication history and easier audit; better continuity of care at discharge.
- Data for research, stock planning and cost control.

**Problems:** cost and training, system downtime, "alert fatigue" when too many warnings appear, and new errors such as choosing the wrong item from a drop-down list.

## 3.7 Barcode medicine identification and automated dispensing

### Barcode medicine identification

A **barcode** stores a product's code as a pattern of bars (linear barcode) or squares (two-dimensional codes such as the DataMatrix or QR code) that a scanner reads. Global standards for product barcodes come from GS1. A 2D code can also carry the batch number and expiry date. Indian rules now also require a QR code on the labels of active pharmaceutical ingredients and of specified leading formulation brands, to help detect fake medicines.

**Barcode medication administration (BCMA)** in hospitals:

1. The nurse scans the patient's wristband barcode.
2. The nurse scans the barcode on the medicine.
3. The computer checks the **"rights"** of medication use — right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time — against the electronic order.
4. A warning appears if anything does not match; administration is recorded automatically.

**Uses in the pharmacy:** receiving stock, picking the right product, billing, batch recall, expiry checks and stock counts.

### Automated dispensing

- **Automated dispensing cabinets (ADCs)** — computer-controlled cabinets on wards that release only the drugs ordered for a patient after the nurse logs in; they record who removed what and when, which is useful for controlled drugs.
- **Pharmacy robots** — machines that store, pick and deliver packs to the counter, or count tablets and fill and label containers.
- **Unit-dose packaging machines** — pack each dose separately with the patient's name and barcode.

**Benefits:** fewer picking errors, faster dispensing, better stock control and security, and more pharmacist time for patient care. **Limitations:** high cost, maintenance, and errors if the machine is loaded wrongly.

## 3.8 Mobile technology and adherence monitoring

**Adherence** means taking medicines as agreed with the prescriber. Poor adherence leads to treatment failure, resistance (in tuberculosis and HIV) and extra cost. Mobile technology (**mHealth**) helps:

- **Reminder apps and SMS** messages at dose times; refill reminders.
- **Electronic pill bottles and caps** (medication event monitoring systems) that record each opening with date and time.
- **Smart pill boxes** that light up or beep and alert a family member if a dose is missed.
- **Video-observed therapy** — the patient records or shows taking the dose (used in tuberculosis programmes).
- **Tele-pharmacy and teleconsultation** — counselling by phone or video.
- **Wearables** linked to apps (glucose and blood pressure readings shared with the care team).
- Apps that hold the patient's medicine list, allergies and pill images.

Problems include privacy of health data, cost, low smartphone or digital literacy in some patients, and reminders being ignored over time.

## 3.9 Diagnostic system

A **computer-aided diagnostic system** helps a doctor reach a diagnosis.

- **Expert systems** store medical knowledge as rules ("IF fever AND neck stiffness THEN consider meningitis"). An early example was MYCIN, built in the 1970s for choosing antibiotics in infections.
- **Computer-aided detection in imaging** — software marks suspicious areas on X-ray, CT or MRI images for the radiologist.
- **Decision support** in ECG machines that print an interpretation, and symptom-checker programs.

Such systems support, but do not replace, the clinician's judgement.

## 3.10 Lab-diagnostic system

A **laboratory diagnostic system (laboratory information system, LIS)** manages clinical laboratory work:

- Test ordering from the ward, barcode labelling of samples, sample tracking.
- Automatic analysers (haematology, biochemistry) connected to the computer send results directly, avoiding copying errors.
- Checking results against reference ranges and flagging abnormal or critical values.
- Quality control charts, result validation and printing or sending reports to the doctor's screen.
- Storage of past results for comparison.

## 3.11 Patient monitoring system

A **patient monitoring system** continuously measures and displays a patient's vital signs, mainly in ICU, operation theatres and emergency wards.

- Parameters: heart rate and ECG, blood pressure (non-invasive and arterial), oxygen saturation (SpO2), respiratory rate, temperature, end-tidal CO2.
- Sensors send signals to a bedside monitor; values and waveforms are displayed and stored.
- **Alarms** sound when a value crosses a set limit.
- A **central station** lets one nurse watch many beds; data can feed into the electronic record.
- **Remote monitoring** sends readings from the patient's home by Internet or phone (heart failure, diabetes, implanted devices).

## 3.12 Pharma information system

A **pharma (pharmaceutical) information system** is the set of computer systems used to manage information in a pharmaceutical company or pharmacy organisation.

| Area | What it manages |
| --- | --- |
| Research and development | Compound and study data, laboratory notebooks, literature |
| Regulatory affairs | Dossiers for approval, product registrations, submissions |
| Manufacturing | Batch records, production planning, ERP (enterprise resource planning) |
| Quality control and assurance | LIMS, deviations, change control, document control |
| Sales and marketing | Distribution, sales analysis, field force reports |
| Pharmacovigilance | Adverse event case processing and reporting |
| Supply chain | Inventory, warehouse, track and trace |

**Benefits:** quick, correct decisions; less paperwork; compliance with good manufacturing and good laboratory practice; traceability of every batch.

## Remember

- Drug information retrieval: search databases with keywords and Boolean operators (AND narrows, OR widens, NOT excludes).
- Pharmacokinetics: computers calculate AUC, k, t½ = 0.693/k, clearance; fit models; simulate doses; support TDM.
- Drug design: QSAR (Hansch: π, σ, Es), molecular modelling, docking, virtual screening, pharmacophores, ADMET prediction.
- Hospital pharmacy: inventory, unit-dose dispensing, patient profiles, interaction alerts, ADR reporting.
- EP systems remove illegible handwriting and add automatic checks; e-discharge improves continuity of care.
- Barcode medication administration checks the rights of patient, drug, dose, route and time.
- Automated dispensing cabinets and robots cut picking errors.
- Mobile adherence tools: reminders, electronic pill caps, smart boxes, video-observed therapy.
- Diagnostic, lab-diagnostic, patient monitoring and pharma information systems support, not replace, professionals.

# Unit 4: Bioinformatics

Modern biology produces huge amounts of data: whole genomes, protein sequences and three-dimensional protein structures. **Bioinformatics** uses computers to store, search and make sense of these data. For pharmacy it matters because drug targets, disease genes and vaccine candidates are now found by searching databases before any experiment is done. This unit covers the introduction, objectives, databases and core concepts of bioinformatics and its impact on vaccine discovery.

## 4.1 Introduction and definition

**Bioinformatics** is the field that applies computer science, mathematics and statistics to biological data, especially DNA, RNA and protein sequences and structures, in order to store them, retrieve them, analyse them and interpret what they mean.

It combines three subjects:

```text
          BIOLOGY
     (genes, proteins,
       cells, disease)
            /\
           /  \
          / BIO-\
         /INFOR- \
        / MATICS  \
       /____________\
 COMPUTER          MATHEMATICS
 SCIENCE           AND STATISTICS
 (databases,       (algorithms, probability,
  programming)      scoring)
```

**Why it grew**

- DNA sequencing became faster and cheaper; the **Human Genome Project** (completed in 2003) produced the sequence of about 3 billion base pairs of human DNA.
- The data are far too large to study by hand.
- The Internet allowed public databases shared by laboratories worldwide.

**Related terms**

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Genome | The complete DNA of an organism |
| Genomics | Study of whole genomes: sequencing, mapping and comparing them |
| Proteome / proteomics | All the proteins made by a cell or organism / their study |
| Transcriptomics | Study of all RNA transcripts (which genes are switched on) |
| Pharmacogenomics | How a person's genes affect their response to drugs |
| Computational biology | Building models and simulations of biological systems (closely overlapping field) |

## 4.2 Objectives of bioinformatics

1. **Organise and store** biological data in databases so that researchers can reach them.
2. **Develop tools and algorithms** to analyse the data (sequence alignment, structure prediction, gene finding).
3. **Analyse and interpret** data to understand biological meaning: gene function, protein structure and evolutionary relationships.
4. **Compare** sequences between species to find related genes and proteins.
5. **Predict** protein structure and function from sequence.
6. **Support drug discovery and vaccine design** by finding targets, antigens and suitable molecules.
7. **Support personalised medicine** by linking genetic differences to disease and drug response.

## 4.3 Concept of bioinformatics

The central idea: biological information flows from DNA to RNA to protein (the **central dogma**), and every step can be read and studied as a sequence of letters.

```text
DNA  (letters A, T, G, C)  ──transcription──►  mRNA (A, U, G, C)
                                                   │ translation
                                                   ▼
                                    Protein (20 amino acids, one-letter codes)
                                                   │ folding
                                                   ▼
                                    3D structure  →  function  →  drug target
```

**Main activities**

1. **Sequence analysis**
   - **Sequence alignment** — lining up two or more sequences to find similar regions. **Pairwise alignment** compares two; **multiple sequence alignment** compares many (Clustal Omega, MUSCLE).
   - **Global alignment** compares sequences over their whole length (Needleman–Wunsch method); **local alignment** finds the best matching part (Smith–Waterman method).
   - **Database similarity searching** with **BLAST** (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) or FASTA finds sequences in a database that resemble a query sequence.
   - **Homology** — similar sequences often come from a common ancestor and have similar functions, so the function of a new gene can be guessed from a known one.
2. **Gene finding and annotation** — locating genes in a raw genome and labelling what they do.
3. **Phylogenetic analysis** — building evolutionary trees from sequences to show how organisms or strains are related (used to trace virus outbreaks).
4. **Structural bioinformatics** — predicting the 3D shape of proteins (homology modelling; machine-learning structure prediction tools), studying binding sites and docking drugs into them.
5. **Functional genomics** — studying gene expression (microarrays, RNA sequencing).
6. **Systems biology** — modelling networks of genes, proteins and metabolic pathways.

**File format example — FASTA** (a common text format for sequences):

```text
>sp|P01308|INS_HUMAN Insulin
MALWMRLLPLLALLALWGPDPAAAFVNQHLCGSHLVEALYLVCGERGFFYTPKT...
```

The first line starts with ">" and gives the identifier and description; the following lines give the sequence.

## 4.4 Bioinformatics databases

A **biological database** is an organised, searchable collection of biological data, usually free online.

### Classification

| Type | What it holds | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Primary (archival) databases** | Original data submitted directly by researchers (raw sequences, structures) | GenBank, ENA, DDBJ, Protein Data Bank (PDB) |
| **Secondary (derived) databases** | Information derived from primary data after analysis: patterns, motifs, domains, families | PROSITE, Pfam, PRINTS, InterPro |
| **Composite databases** | Combine several primary databases into one search | UniProt (partly), NCBI's linked databases |
| **Specialised databases** | Focus on one organism, disease or data type | OMIM (human genetic disorders), KEGG (pathways), DrugBank (drugs and targets), IEDB (immune epitopes) |
| **Literature databases** | Published articles | PubMed |

### Nucleotide sequence databases

The three main DNA databases exchange data every day as the **International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC)**, so a sequence submitted to one appears in all three:

| Database | Run by |
| --- | --- |
| **GenBank** | NCBI (National Center for Biotechnology Information), USA |
| **ENA** (European Nucleotide Archive) | EMBL–EBI (European Bioinformatics Institute), UK |
| **DDBJ** (DNA Data Bank of Japan) | National Institute of Genetics, Japan |

### Protein databases

- **UniProt** — the main protein sequence and function resource. It contains **UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot** (manually reviewed and annotated, high quality) and **UniProtKB/TrEMBL** (automatically annotated, not reviewed).
- **PDB (Protein Data Bank)** — 3D structures of proteins and nucleic acids solved by X-ray crystallography, NMR and cryo-electron microscopy. Each structure has a four-character PDB ID.
- **PROSITE** and **Pfam** — protein families, domains and functional patterns.

### Other useful resources

| Resource | Use |
| --- | --- |
| NCBI Entrez | One search across many NCBI databases (nucleotide, protein, PubMed, gene) |
| KEGG | Metabolic and signalling pathways, diseases, drugs |
| OMIM | Human genes and genetic disorders |
| PubChem | Small molecules and their biological activities |
| DrugBank | Drugs with their targets, mechanisms and interactions |
| BLAST (tool at NCBI) | Finding similar sequences |

**Uses of databases in pharmacy:** finding the sequence and structure of a drug target, checking whether a target exists in humans (to avoid side effects of antimicrobial drugs), finding gene variants that change drug metabolism (pharmacogenomics), and searching for antigens for vaccines.

## 4.5 Applications of bioinformatics (overview)

- **Drug discovery** — target identification and validation, virtual screening, structure-based design.
- **Pharmacogenomics and personalised medicine** — dose or drug chosen by the patient's genes (for example variants of drug-metabolising enzymes).
- **Vaccine discovery** — see 4.6.
- **Diagnosis** — identifying disease-causing mutations and pathogens by their sequences.
- **Microbiology** — tracking resistance genes and outbreak strains.
- **Agriculture and biotechnology** — improved crops, enzyme engineering.
- **Evolution studies** — comparing genomes across species.

## 4.6 Impact of bioinformatics in vaccine discovery

A **vaccine** contains an antigen (or the genetic code for it) that trains the immune system to recognise a pathogen. The classical way of making vaccines (grow the organism, then kill or weaken it, or purify its parts) is slow and fails for organisms that cannot be grown easily or that vary a lot. Bioinformatics has changed vaccine discovery in several ways.

### 1. Reverse vaccinology

Instead of starting in the laboratory, scientists **start from the pathogen's genome** on the computer:

```text
Sequence the pathogen genome
        ↓
Predict all the proteins (open reading frames)
        ↓
Select likely antigens by computer:
  - surface-exposed or secreted proteins (signal peptides, membrane anchors)
  - present in many strains (conserved)
  - not similar to human proteins (to avoid autoimmunity)
        ↓
Make the selected proteins and test them in animals
        ↓
Best candidates go to vaccine development
```

Reverse vaccinology was first used successfully for **Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B** (meningococcus B), whose surface sugar could not be used as an antigen; computer screening of its genome found protein antigens that were later used in a licensed vaccine.

### 2. Epitope prediction (immunoinformatics)

An **epitope** is the small part of an antigen recognised by an antibody (B-cell epitope) or by a T cell (T-cell epitope, presented on HLA/MHC molecules). Programs predict which peptides are likely to be epitopes, and which HLA types will present them, so that **epitope-based** or **multi-epitope vaccines** can be designed. The **Immune Epitope Database (IEDB)** stores known epitopes and prediction tools.

### 3. Comparing strains and tracking variation

Alignment and phylogenetic trees show which parts of a pathogen stay the same across strains (good vaccine targets) and which keep changing. This is used every year to choose **influenza** strains for the seasonal vaccine and to watch new variants of viruses.

### 4. Faster vaccines for new diseases

When a new virus appears, its genome can be sequenced and shared in public databases within days. During the COVID-19 pandemic the SARS-CoV-2 sequence was shared publicly early in 2020, and developers used it directly to design **mRNA** and viral-vector vaccines encoding the spike protein, without needing to grow the virus first.

### 5. Structure-based vaccine design

3D structures (PDB) and modelling help engineer antigens that keep the shape the immune system should recognise (for example stabilising a viral protein in its pre-fusion form).

### 6. Safety and other uses

- Checking candidate antigens for similarity to human proteins and for allergen-like sequences.
- Predicting population coverage of epitopes across HLA types.
- Analysing immune responses in trials and monitoring vaccine effectiveness against new strains.

**Benefits of bioinformatics in vaccine discovery:** faster discovery (years reduced), lower cost, ability to target organisms that cannot be cultured, wider strain coverage and more rational, safer design. **Limitation:** every computer prediction must still be confirmed in the laboratory, in animals and in clinical trials.

## Remember

- Bioinformatics = biology + computer science + mathematics/statistics applied to sequence and structure data.
- Objectives: store, develop tools, analyse, compare, predict structure/function, aid drug and vaccine discovery.
- Central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein → structure → function.
- Alignment: pairwise vs multiple; global (Needleman–Wunsch) vs local (Smith–Waterman); BLAST searches databases.
- Primary databases: GenBank (NCBI), ENA (EMBL–EBI), DDBJ (Japan) — INSDC; PDB for structures. Secondary: PROSITE, Pfam. UniProt: Swiss-Prot (reviewed) + TrEMBL (unreviewed).
- Vaccine discovery: reverse vaccinology (meningococcus B), epitope prediction (IEDB), strain comparison (influenza), rapid genome sharing (COVID-19 mRNA vaccines), structure-based antigen design.

# Unit 5: Computers as data analysis in preclinical development

Before a new drug can be given to people, it goes through **preclinical development**: laboratory and animal studies of its chemistry, formulation, stability, pharmacology, pharmacokinetics and toxicity. These studies produce very large amounts of data, and regulators must be able to trust every number. This unit covers the three computer systems named in the syllabus: the **chromatography data system (CDS)**, the **laboratory information management system (LIMS)** and the **text information management system (TIMS)**, together with the data-integrity rules they must follow.

## 5.1 Preclinical development and the need for computers

| Preclinical activity | Data produced |
| --- | --- |
| Characterisation of the drug substance | Spectra, chromatograms, impurity profiles |
| Formulation development | Dissolution profiles, content uniformity, physical tests |
| Stability studies | Assay and impurity results at many time points and storage conditions |
| Bioanalysis | Drug levels in plasma of test animals (LC–MS/MS, HPLC) |
| Pharmacology and toxicology | Doses, observations, body weights, clinical pathology, histopathology |
| Reports and submissions | Study protocols, final reports, summaries for the regulator |

**Why computers are needed**

- The volume of data is too large for paper notebooks.
- Calculations (peak areas, calibration curves, statistics) must be accurate and repeatable.
- Results must be **traceable**: who did what, when, on which instrument.
- Studies must follow **Good Laboratory Practice (GLP)**, under which raw data, records and reports are kept so the study can be reconstructed later.
- Data must be ready to submit to regulators and easy to retrieve years later.

### Data integrity: ALCOA

Regulators expect computerised records to be **ALCOA** (often extended to ALCOA+):

| Letter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| A — Attributable | Each entry shows who made it and when |
| L — Legible | Readable and permanent |
| C — Contemporaneous | Recorded at the time the work is done |
| O — Original | The first record (or a verified true copy) is kept |
| A — Accurate | Correct and free of errors; changes are explained |
| "+" | Complete, consistent, enduring and available |

In the USA, **21 CFR Part 11** sets the rules for electronic records and electronic signatures; laboratories that supply data for global submissions design their systems to meet it. Key features required: unique user logins, **audit trails** (a secure, time-stamped record of every creation, change and deletion with the reason), electronic signatures, access control, validation of the software, and secure backup and archiving.

## 5.2 Chromatographic data system (CDS)

**Chromatography** (HPLC, GC, UPLC, LC–MS) is the most used analytical technique in pharmaceutical analysis: assay, related substances, dissolution, stability and bioanalysis. The detector gives an electrical signal over time; a **chromatography data system** is the software that **controls the instrument and collects, processes, stores and reports** these data.

### Functions of a CDS

```text
 Instrument control  →  Data acquisition  →  Processing  →  Reporting  →  Storage / review
 (pump flow, oven       (signal vs time      (peak detection,  (results,     (secure database,
  temperature,           stored as raw        integration,      system        audit trail,
  injection sequence)    data file)           calibration)      suitability)  approval)
```

1. **Instrument control** — sets flow rate, gradient, column temperature, detector wavelength and injection volume; runs a **sequence** of standards and samples automatically, overnight if needed.
2. **Data acquisition** — records the detector signal against time and stores it as an unchangeable raw-data file.
3. **Peak detection and integration** — finds where each peak starts and ends, draws the baseline and calculates **retention time**, **peak area** and **peak height**. Integration parameters (threshold, peak width) are set in a processing method; manual integration is allowed only with justification and is recorded in the audit trail.
4. **Calibration and calculation** — builds a calibration curve from standards (external or internal standard method), calculates concentrations, % assay, % impurities and % dissolved.
5. **System suitability** — calculates theoretical plates (column efficiency), tailing factor, resolution between peaks and % RSD of replicate injections, and checks them against limits before results are accepted.
6. **Reporting** — prints or exports results with chromatograms, summary tables and pass/fail against specifications.
7. **Review and approval** — results are reviewed and signed electronically by an analyst and a reviewer.
8. **Security and compliance** — user roles, password control, audit trail, prevention of deleting or overwriting raw data, and archiving.

**Networked CDS:** in large laboratories, many instruments connect to a central server, so data are stored centrally and reviewers can work from any desk. Common commercial CDS products include Empower (Waters), Chromeleon (Thermo Fisher) and OpenLab (Agilent).

### Advantages of a CDS

- Accurate, reproducible integration and calculations; no manual errors in reading charts.
- Unattended operation of long sequences saves time.
- Raw data and every change are traceable (audit trail) — essential in GLP and GMP inspections.
- Quick comparison of chromatograms, trend analysis and easy retrieval of old data.
- Results can be passed electronically to a LIMS.

## 5.3 Laboratory information management system (LIMS)

A **LIMS** is software that manages the **samples, tests, results, people and instruments** of a laboratory and the **workflow** that links them. Where a CDS handles data from one type of instrument, a LIMS manages the whole laboratory's operations.

### Sample life cycle in a LIMS

```text
 Sample login        →  Labelling     →  Test assignment  →  Analysis   →  Result entry
 (registered with        (barcode)       (tests from the     (on the       (manual, or directly
  unique ID, source,                      specification;       instrument)   from instruments/CDS)
  batch, date)                            work given to analyst)
        →  Calculation and check against specification  →  Review and approval
        →  Report / certificate of analysis  →  Storage, archive and disposal of the sample
```

### Functions

| Function | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Sample management | Registration, barcode labels, location tracking, chain of custody |
| Test and specification management | Stores test methods and limits for each product; flags out-of-specification (OOS) results automatically |
| Workload and scheduling | Assigns work to analysts and instruments, shows pending tests and due dates |
| Instrument integration | Takes results directly from balances, pH meters, CDS and other instruments |
| Stability study management | Plans pull points (e.g. 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 months) under each storage condition, reminds when samples are due, trends results |
| Inventory | Reference standards, reagents, columns, with expiry dates |
| Instrument management | Calibration and maintenance schedules; blocks use of an out-of-calibration instrument |
| Quality records | Deviations, OOS investigations, training records of analysts |
| Reporting | Certificates of analysis, trend charts, management reports |
| Compliance | Audit trail, electronic signatures, user access levels (21 CFR Part 11, GLP/GMP) |

### Advantages of a LIMS

- Less paperwork and fewer transcription errors.
- Faster turnaround time and better use of analysts and instruments.
- Full traceability of each sample and result; easy audits.
- Automatic checking against limits and quick detection of trends.
- Data shared with other company systems (ERP for batch release, document systems).

**Limitations:** high cost, time to configure and validate, staff training, and dependence on the system (downtime procedures needed). Examples of commercial LIMS include LabWare, STARLIMS and LabVantage.

### CDS vs LIMS

| CDS | LIMS |
| --- | --- |
| Handles chromatography instruments and their data | Handles the whole laboratory's samples, tests and workflow |
| Raw data: signals, chromatograms, peak areas | Results, specifications, sample status, reports |
| Focus on acquisition and processing | Focus on management, tracking and reporting |
| Sends final results to the LIMS | Receives results from the CDS and other instruments |

## 5.4 Text information management system (TIMS)

Much of the information in drug development is **unstructured text**, not numbers in tables: study protocols, laboratory reports, standard operating procedures (SOPs), literature articles, regulatory documents, correspondence and scientists' notes. A **text information management system** stores, organises, indexes and retrieves such text documents.

### Functions

1. **Capture and storage** — documents entered in electronic form or scanned (with optical character recognition to make scanned text searchable).
2. **Indexing** — each document is tagged with keywords and details (title, author, date, study number, compound, document type) so it can be found later.
3. **Full-text search and retrieval** — searching inside documents by words or phrases, with Boolean operators, filters and ranking.
4. **Version control** — keeps every version of a document (draft, reviewed, approved, superseded) so only the current approved version is used.
5. **Workflow** — routes documents for review and approval with electronic signatures.
6. **Security** — access only to authorised users; audit trail of who viewed or changed a document.
7. **Text mining** — software that reads large collections of text (such as published literature or adverse event narratives) to find patterns, for example new drug–side-effect associations or links between genes and diseases.
8. **Archiving** — long-term secure storage, as GLP requires study records to be retained.

### Uses in preclinical development

- Managing study protocols, amendments and final reports of toxicology and pharmacology studies.
- Keeping SOPs, specifications and test methods under document control.
- Literature searching and storing references for the drug.
- Preparing regulatory documents by reusing approved text.
- Searching past reports to avoid repeating experiments.

**Related systems:** **electronic laboratory notebooks (ELN)**, which replace paper lab notebooks, and **document management systems (DMS)** used for SOPs and regulatory dossiers. Together with CDS and LIMS they make up the paperless laboratory.

```text
                ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
                │   Preclinical data analysis by computers  │
                └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
       ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────┬────────────────────┐
       ▼                  ▼                      ▼                    ▼
     CDS                LIMS                   TIMS               ELN / DMS
 chromatography     samples, tests,       text documents:      experiments,
 raw data and       results, workflow,    protocols, reports,  SOPs and
 calculations       stability, CoA        SOPs, literature     controlled docs
       └──────── results flow ──────►┘
```

## 5.5 Other computer tools in preclinical data analysis

- **Statistical software** (SAS, R, SPSS, GraphPad Prism) — analysing dose–response, comparing treated and control animal groups, calculating LD50 or ED50 and confidence intervals.
- **Pharmacokinetic software** — calculating AUC, Cmax and half-life in animal studies to choose doses for first-in-human trials.
- **Toxicology data systems** — recording animal observations, body weights and pathology findings directly at the bench.
- **Standard electronic formats** for submitting non-clinical study data to regulators (such as the SEND standard used by the US FDA).

## Remember

- Preclinical studies follow GLP; computer records must be ALCOA (attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate).
- Part 11 features: unique logins, audit trail, electronic signatures, validation, secure backup.
- CDS: instrument control → acquisition → peak integration → calibration and calculation → system suitability → report → secure storage.
- LIMS: sample login, barcodes, test assignment, instrument interface, OOS flags, stability scheduling, certificates of analysis, audit trail.
- TIMS: stores, indexes and searches unstructured text (protocols, reports, SOPs, literature); version control; text mining.
- CDS feeds results to LIMS; TIMS, ELN and DMS handle the documents.
